tasks.objective: Teach the roadmap parser one more bullet, `- error_issues:`, so a project can say once that its issue tracker is not to be written to. The roadmap is already this factory's project register -- `projects.ts`'s own header says the `- project:` bullets ARE the register -- so this adds no second source of truth. Mechanically it is one more `bulletValue()` call in the loop that already reads `id`, `status`, `goal`, `epics`, `project` and `kind`, one more field on `MilestoneDef`, one default, and one project-wide resolution pass. The precedent to follow is `kind`, not `status`: like `kind`, this bullet describes a PROJECT while being written on a MILESTONE, so one bullet has to settle every milestone naming that project, and an explicit disagreement is a refusal rather than a precedence rule -- `resolveKinds`'s own docblock argues there is no reading of two different values for one project more likely than a typo. The default is ON, because the epic's goal says default ON; and a value the parser cannot read must REFUSE, never degrade to that default, because `parseEpicIds`'s docblock records exactly that bug (an unreadable value arriving downstream as a deliberate declaration) and records that the fix was to refuse. This task ships the parser and the reader only. It writes no `- error_issues:` bullet onto any real milestone, it touches no consumer, and it deliberately does not know that GitHub exists.

tasks.objective: Build the pure core of the mechanism as a new module, `factory/orchestrator/src/errorIssues.ts`: fold the event log into a list of reportable errors, give each one a stable fingerprint, and render the issue title and body. It folds the LOG, not the call sites, and that is the single most load-bearing decision in this epic. The three error sources named by the goal -- a `gate-outcome` whose outcome is `blocked`, a task that reaches `task_status: failed`, and every `error-logged` event -- share no call site, and `error-logged` is routinely written BY HAND by the orchestrator through `smith event append` (the dispatch contract in `.claude/skills/bs/SKILL.md` says so outright: emit it "never from inside the agent"), which no in-process hook can ever observe. All three sources do share one writer, `appendEvent`, and therefore one reader: the log. A producer built as three hooks covers at most two sources and silently misses the third; a fold covers all three uniformly and needs no edit to `gate.ts`, `queue.ts` or `taskEvents.ts`. The module is pure by contract: no filesystem, no network, no child process, no clock. Events arrive as a parameter, the current time arrives as a parameter, and WHETHER A PROJECT IS ENABLED ARRIVES AS A PARAMETER -- this module never reads the roadmap, which is what lets it be built in the same wave as the roadmap bullet rather than behind it.
acceptance_criteria: TDD, and the null is a REAL rival implementation rather than a missing file. FIRST write a test that folds a fixture log of three events -- one `gate-outcome` with `outcome: blocked`, one event that yields `task_status: failed`, and one HAND-APPENDED `error-logged` that carries no dispatch context, no session start and no surrounding task events -- and asserts the fold returns exactly 3 reports. Run it, watch it fail, record the failure text verbatim. Under the null of a hook-shaped implementation the third event is invisible and the count is 2; under the hypothesis it is 3. State both numbers in the Result. `2 !== 3` is the differential, and it is the reason this module exists.

The five-rounds test, which is fork 1's whole point. A fixture log carries the SAME gate blocking with the SAME reason on the SAME task across five different sessions, five different plan versions and five different timestamps. The fold returns five reports and EXACTLY ONE distinct fingerprint. Under the null -- a fingerprint including session, plan version or timestamp -- it returns five distinct fingerprints. Paste both the distinct-fingerprint count and the fingerprint value into the Result.

The fingerprint discriminates where it must. Changing the task id, the error class, or the project each produces a DIFFERENT fingerprint from the baseline; the test asserts four distinct values and prints them. A fingerprint that never changes would pass the previous criterion and fail this one, which is why both are here.

All ten gate reasons are mapped, and the test reads the ten FROM THE SOURCE rather than restating them. A table-driven test enumerates the blocked-arm reason vocabulary by importing it from `gate.ts` (or, if it is not exported, by asserting against a list the test derives from the type and the test says how), and asserts each maps to `gate.blocked.<reason>` with no reason falling through to a default. Under the null -- a hand-copied list of ten strings in the test -- an eleventh reason added later maps to nothing and the suite stays green. Under the hypothesis the suite goes red the day the vocabulary grows. Say in the Result which of the two you were able to build and, if the vocabulary could not be imported, why.

Neither renderer can carry a payload, and the comment is tested exactly as hard as the body. A test constructs a source event whose `detail` contains the literal string `SECRETLIKE-abc123` and a fenced diff hunk, folds it, renders BOTH the body and the comment, and asserts for EACH that `includes('SECRETLIKE-abc123')` is false and that no line starts with `+` or `-`. A second pair of tests adds an UNKNOWN extra field to the source event payload and asserts the rendered body AND the rendered comment are each byte-identical to the run without it. Under the null of a filter-based redactor the unknown field appears in the output; under the allowlist construction it cannot. Paste both rendered artifacts verbatim into the Result -- they are metadata only, so quoting them is safe, and quoting them is the evidence. A test that covers the body and not the comment does not satisfy this criterion: the comment is the path that runs four times as often.

The comment renderer has no free-text door. `grep -n "renderComment" factory/orchestrator/src/errorIssues.ts` shows its signature; paste it. Assert in a test that its parameter type has no field typed `string` that is fed from a source event's `detail` -- concretely, a test constructs the typed record from a folded report and asserts the record's key set, sorted, equals a literal list pasted in the Result. Under the null the record carries a `detail` or a `text` field and the assertion names it.

Purity is checked by an instrument that can fail. `grep -nE "node:fs|node:child_process|require\\(|fetch\\(|Date\\.now|new Date\\(\\)" factory/orchestrator/src/errorIssues.ts` returns no lines; paste the command and its empty output. Then a test calls the fold twice with identical input and asserts `JSON.stringify` equality of the two results.

A malformed event does not kill the fold. A test folds a log containing one event with a missing payload field and one valid event, and asserts one report is returned AND that the skipped count in the return value is 1. Under the null the fold throws and returns nothing; the difference between `{reports: 1, skipped: 1}` and an exception is the criterion.
`scripts/check.sh` run whole, tail pasted with suite counts and every SKIP named. Claims respected: `git diff --name-only` pasted, listing only this task's claims.

functional_clauses: The fold covers all three sources in one pass over the event sequence. Source 1: an event of type `gate-outcome` whose payload `outcome` is `blocked` (the blocked arm's `reason` is one of exactly ten strings, defined in `gate.ts` as `GateOutcome`'s blocked arm). Source 2: `error-logged`, whatever wrote it -- an in-process `emitTaskBlocked` call or a hand-appended event carrying no dispatch context at all. Source 3: the event or events whose projection puts a task at `task_status: failed`; `failed` is a member of the projector's status list in `db/projector.ts`, and this task's FIRST research step is to read that projection, determine exactly which event type or types produce that status, cite them by path and by a quotable string, and fold every one of them. If more than one event type can produce it, all are folded. If the status turns out to be derived from something that is not an event, the Result says so plainly and names what it is instead -- that is a finding, not a licence to cover two sources out of three.

No producer call site is edited. `gate.ts`, `queue.ts`, `taskEvents.ts`, `events.ts` and `escalation.ts` are not in this task's claims and are not touched. The module's input is a sequence of already-read stored events.

The fingerprint is exactly this and is written down as such: the first 16 hex characters of a SHA-256 over the NUL-joined tuple `project`, `source`, `error_class`, `task_ref`. It DELIBERATELY EXCLUDES session id, epic id, plan version, event id, timestamp and detail, and the module's docblock says why in one sentence: the failure the operator named is one broken gate repeating across five rounds opening five issues, and session, plan version and timestamp are precisely the fields that change between those rounds. A fingerprint that includes any of them would be correct-looking and would open five issues.

The error class mapping is stated per source, for all three. `gate-outcome` blocked has no error class of its own -- it has a `reason` from a closed set of ten -- so it maps to `gate.blocked.<reason>`. `error-logged` carries a taxonomy error class in its payload's `error` field (`group.class`, e.g. `execution.test-failure`), which is used verbatim. A failed task maps to `task.failed`, extended with the discriminator the source event carries if it carries one, and the module names which. The mapping is a table in the source, not scattered conditionals.

The rendered issue body is METADATA AND POINTERS ONLY, and is safe by CONSTRUCTION rather than by filtering. The renderer takes a typed record with a fixed, named set of fields -- event id, task id, error class, severity, session, epic, plan version, project, source -- plus the literal `smith event` command an operator runs locally to read the detail. WHICH event id it carries is stated rather than left to the implementer: it is `latest_event_id`, the NEWEST contributing event id in the fingerprint's group, not the first one seen and not an arbitrary member -- a fingerprint deliberately groups many events (clause 3), so `the event id` is ambiguous until this sentence disambiguates it, and the newest is the one that answers `has anything happened since we last reported`. The fold therefore exports `latest_event_id` as a named field on every report it returns, which is where task 4's reporter gets it from -- the reporter never rescans the log for it and never recomputes it, it reads the field off the report and writes it into the `issue-reported` payload (task 4 clause 6) so the next run can compare against it (task 4 clause 2, step 4). It never receives the raw payload, so there is nothing for a filter to miss. No quoted log, no diff, no `detail` field, no payload text, ever. `docs/standards/guardrails.md` describes a secret-redacting event logger that this repository DOES NOT HAVE (`appendEvent` validates and appends; it scrubs nothing), and this construction is what makes a metadata-only body safe without one. Do not build a redactor and do not depend on one.

The body carries one machine-readable fingerprint line, in a fixed literal format the module exports as a constant so the dedup search and the renderer cannot drift apart. It is the only thing a searcher is allowed to match on.

There are TWO renderers, not one, and they are the same construction. `renderComment()` sits beside `renderBody()` and takes the SAME typed record of named fields -- never a raw payload, never a source event. The comment is what the dedup path writes, and the dedup path is the HIGHER-VOLUME write path (five rounds of one broken gate produce one body and four comments), so the allowlist-by-construction guarantee that makes the body safe has to cover it by the same mechanism rather than by prose. `renderComment()`'s field set is: the new occurrence's event id, its timestamp, its session, its epic, its plan version, the same fingerprint line constant, and the literal `smith event` command an operator runs locally to read the detail. No `detail`, no quoted log line, no diff, no summary composed from payload text. If a caller wants to say more, it adds a NAMED FIELD to the record type and the renderer prints it -- there is no free-text parameter to abuse.
The title is stable, human-first, and derived only from allowlisted fields.
The module is pure. It imports no `node:fs`, no `node:child_process`, no fetch, and calls no clock: `now` is a parameter. Two calls with the same input return byte-identical output.
Enablement is a parameter, not a lookup. The fold takes the set of enabled projects (or a predicate) from its caller and never imports `roadmap.ts`.
nonfunctional_clauses: Nothing in this module may throw on a malformed event. The log is append-only and holds events written by hand; an event this fold cannot understand is SKIPPED and COUNTED, and the count is part of the fold's return value. A fold that dies on one bad row is silent exactly when something is already wrong.
The module performs no I/O whatsoever, which is also its security boundary: it cannot leak what it cannot read.

tasks.objective: Build the second half of the pure core: resolving WHICH GitHub repository a project directory belongs to, classifying whether `gh` can be used at all, and composing the exact argv of every `gh` command this epic will ever run -- all behind an INJECTABLE command runner so that no test in this epic ever touches a real tracker. This is new code, not a reuse: the one occurrence of `gh` under `factory/orchestrator/src` is `scaffold.ts`, and it merely COMPOSES A COMMAND STRING for the operator to run; nothing in this repository has ever shelled out to `gh`, and nothing reads a git remote -- `git.ts` exports exactly four things, `GitCommandError`, `redactCredentials`, `runGit` and `runGitRaw`. The runner exists because of a hard constraint on this epic: no task may run `gh issue create` against a real repository as part of its own acceptance. Opening a real issue to prove the code opens issues is not a test; it is a side effect on the operator's tracker that no gate can undo. So the deliverable is a pair of pure command BUILDERS plus a runner interface, and the thing every test asserts on is the argv that WOULD have been run.
acceptance_criteria: TDD and differential. FIRST write a table-driven test over the five remote URL forms asserting each yields the slug `o/r`, run it, watch it fail, record the failure text verbatim. Under the null the module does not resolve or the function returns the raw URL; under the hypothesis all five rows return the identical string `o/r`. Paste the five inputs and five outputs into the Result.

Refusal is distinguishable from an answer. Three tests -- a temp directory that is not a git repo, a git repo with no `origin`, and a repo whose `origin` is `https://gitlab.com/o/r.git` -- each assert a typed refusal whose reason names which of the three happened, and assert the three reasons are three DIFFERENT strings. Under the null all three return `null` and the caller cannot tell them apart; the criterion is that the three recorded strings differ from each other, and the Result pastes all three.

Credentials never survive. A test resolves `https://user:ghp_FAKETOKEN123@github.com/o/r.git`, asserts the slug is `o/r`, and asserts that the literal `ghp_FAKETOKEN123` appears in NO field of the returned value and in no message of any error raised on that path. Under the null the token rides along inside an error string that is later written to an event or an issue. The test asserts absence of that exact literal.

Two projects, two directories, two slugs -- and the third project gets nothing. A table-driven test builds a register with two entries pointing at two temporary directories whose stubbed `origin` remotes differ (`https://github.com/juzser/blacksmith.git` and `git@github.com:someone/demo-rpg.git`) and asserts `resolveProjectRepo` returns `juzser/blacksmith` for the first name and `someone/demo-rpg` for the second -- two names in one assertion, because a resolver that ignores its argument passes any single-project test. A third case asks for a project name the register does not carry and asserts the return is the typed refusal `no-checkout`; paste the refusal value verbatim. Under the null -- a resolver that falls back to the process's own directory -- the third case returns `juzser/blacksmith` and reads exactly like a success. That difference, `no-checkout` versus `juzser/blacksmith`, is the criterion, and it is the difference between refusing and filing another project's failure on the operator's own tracker.

`gh` classification produces three distinguishable answers. A stub runner is driven three ways -- a spawn failure carrying an ENOENT-shaped error, exit status 1 with stderr containing a not-logged-in message, exit status 0 -- and the three results are asserted to be three DIFFERENT named outcomes. Under the null of a boolean the first two both read `false` and the operator is told `gh unavailable` when the real remedy is `gh auth login`. The Result pastes all three outcome names.

The builders are argv and survive hostile text. A test builds a create-issue command whose body contains a backtick, `$(id)`, a newline and a double quote, and asserts the composed argv is an ARRAY, that the body reaches its destination byte-for-byte, and that no element of the argv contains a composed shell fragment. Then `grep -nE "shell: *true|execSync|exec\\(" ` over the module returns nothing but the allowlisted `execFileSync`; paste the grep and its output.

Nothing was run. The test file for this module imports no `node:child_process`; `grep -n "child_process" factory/orchestrator/test/gh.test.ts` returns nothing, and the stub runner records every call it receives so a test can assert the call COUNT. Paste the recorded argv list from at least one test -- it is the epic's central evidence shape: we assert on what would have been run.
`scripts/check.sh` run whole, tail pasted with counts and SKIPs named. Claims respected: `git diff --name-only` pasted, listing only this task's claims.

functional_clauses: A remote reader is added to `git.ts` beside `runGit`, and it goes through the existing `exec` helper so it inherits that file's whole reason for existing: stderr captured rather than inherited, stdin ignored so an unattended git never blocks on a credential prompt, and failures folded into `GitCommandError` with `redactCredentials` applied. No second `git()` helper is written anywhere.

The remote reader turns a project directory into an `owner/repo` slug, parsing all of: `https://github.com/o/r.git`, `https://github.com/o/r`, `git@github.com:o/r.git`, `ssh://git@github.com/o/r.git`, and an https URL carrying userinfo credentials. The `.git` suffix is stripped. A host that is not GitHub is NOT a slug and is refused, not guessed.

The module answers `WHICH REPOSITORY IS THIS PROJECT'S?`, and answers it from a register handed in rather than from a name lookup. A `resolveProjectRepo(project, register, runner)` takes the project name off a candidate error, a REGISTER of `{name, dir}` entries (the `ProjectRef` shape `projects.ts` already exports -- type-imported, never edited, and never re-derived here), and the injected runner, and returns either an `owner/repo` slug or a typed refusal. `projects.ts:11-20` states the rule this clause exists to honour, verbatim: `PROJECTS_DIR` is this clone's PARENT and on the machine this was written on that parent holds a `black-smith` directory which is a DIFFERENT REPOSITORY WITH A DIFFERENT REMOTE, so a name lookup under the roots would have the factory `read somebody else's lockfile while reporting that it was reading its own`. Therefore: no name lookup, no path guessing, and above all NO FALLBACK TO THE PROCESS'S OWN DIRECTORY. A project the register does not name is refusal `no-checkout`, which is the fifth member of clause 4's refusal set. A resolver that answers with `REPO_ROOT` when it does not know is the well-formed wrong answer D-133 was written about, aimed this time at an outward-facing side effect that cannot be undone by a gate.

Absence is TYPED, never null-as-success, and the set is closed and named: `no-checkout` (the register does not name this project), `not-a-repo` (the directory exists but is not a git repository), `no-origin` (no `origin` remote), `unparseable-remote` (a URL this module cannot parse), and `non-github-host` (a parseable remote whose host is not GitHub). Each carries a reason string and each is a distinct value -- not `null`, not an empty string, not a shared error. D-133's rule governs this whole neighbourhood: a well-formed wrong answer is worse than a refusal, and a caller that cannot tell `no remote` from `not a repo` will report one as the other.

`gh` availability is classified into a closed, named set of at least three distinct outcomes -- ready, missing (the binary is not on PATH), and unauthenticated -- plus an explicit unknown for anything else, each carrying the reason. A boolean is not acceptable: a boolean collapses missing and unauthenticated into one word and makes the operator's remedy unguessable.

The command runner is an injected interface: a function taking a command and an argv array and returning exit status, stdout and stderr, never throwing for a non-zero exit. A default implementation wrapping `execFileSync` ships in the module, in the same shape as `git.ts`'s `exec` (stdio `['ignore','pipe','pipe']`), and every consumer takes the runner as a parameter with the default applied at the edge.
Three pure builders return argv ARRAYS and nothing else: create an issue, search open issues, comment on an issue. They spawn nothing. They are what tests assert on.

argv, never a shell. No builder produces a string to be interpreted; no consumer sets `shell: true`; no string interpolation composes a command. The issue body is delivered through a mechanism that cannot be re-parsed by a shell -- `--body-file` with a temporary file, or stdin -- and the choice is stated with its reason in the module docblock.
Every helper in this module is total: it returns a classified outcome rather than throwing, except for programming errors. Reporting an error must never itself become a second error.
nonfunctional_clauses: SECURITY, explicit because it is the epic's real blast radius: this module composes commands that run under an authenticated `gh` whose token carries `repo` scope.
